did_you_know.text: The command to take seven pairs of clean animals is also connected to what happens after the Flood: Noah offers some of them as a sacrifice in the next chapter. This leaves enough animals for both survival and sacrifice.
The number forty often marks a period of testing or change in the Bible, such as Israel’s forty years in the wilderness and Moses’ forty days on the mountain.
The phrase “the windows of heaven” presents an ancient image of the sky as having openings through which water pours down. The same image appears elsewhere in the Bible.
The phrase “on that very day” emphasizes that the event happened openly and at a clearly marked time. A similar expression is used when describing the Exodus.
The text does not merely say that Noah closed the ark’s door; it says that God closed it for him. This wording presents the closing as an act of protection as well.
The ark is described with the verb “went,” even though it has no sails or steering system. The verb emphasizes that it floats on the waters rather than sailing toward a human-chosen destination.
An ancient cubit was roughly 45 centimeters long, though its length varied in different places. Fifteen cubits would therefore be about seven meters, not an exact modern measurement.

Ancient Mesopotamia, in present-day Iraq, also produced flood stories such as the Atrahasis Epic and the Epic of Gilgamesh. They too include a flood, a hero, and a boat, but each story has its own religious and literary message.
